newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Kuwait bourse could be Gulf centre after reforms.
newsitem.headline: Kuwait bourse could be Gulf centre after reforms.

text.p: The Kuwait Stock Exchange (KSE) could become a regional centre but the Gulf Arab state has first to take three main steps, a World Bank expert said on Tuesday.
Les Nemethy, senior private sector development specialist, told a privatisation seminar in Kuwait that the KSE holds "the reasonable chance of becoming a regional centre in the next few years".

But the task "will not be easy, given the likelihood of keen competition. To improve the chances, the Kuwaiti government and the KSE could take three important steps," Nemethy said in a study presented to the seminar.

Nemethy, who has been working closely with Kuwait's privatisation programme over the past two years, said structural reform and the implementation of the next phase of selling state holdings in utility firms were needed.

He also recommended the removal of restrictions on foreign investment and a reform of securities laws "to better regulate insider trading, and takeovers and to better protect the rights of minority shareholders...
"No financial centre can exclude foreign participation, and aspire to regional pre-eminence," Nemethy added.

Only nationals of Gulf Arab states -- Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Oman and Kuwait -- can trade on the exchange. Kuwait's foreign residents are allowed to take part in mutual funds run by Kuwaiti firms.
Kuwait has said it was considering a plan to remove the ban on foreign participation but no time frame was set.
Kuwait's finance minister, Nasser al-Rodhan, told the seminar that he hoped parliament would approve the next privatisation phase during 1997 to "start preparing public utilities for privatisation".

Nemethy's study praised the Kuwait Investment Authority (KIA), the state investment arm, in privatising holdings worth $2 billion over the past two years which helped create resurgence in capital markets.

He said KSE's index rose over the past two years by about 90 percent while trading value reached 5.3 billion dinars ($17.7 billion) in the first 11 months of 1996 from 584 million in 1994. The buoyant market also resulted in boosting the value of KIA's shares in Kuwaiti firms to $3.9 billion from $2.8 billion.

KSE Director-General Hisham al-Oteibi told the seminar that the bourse recorded in the nine months to September a trade value four times larger than total trading value on seven other official exchanges in fellow Arab states.

KIA Director-General Ali al-Bader told the seminar KSE was becoming one of the most active bourses, recording a trading value in the January-October period as a percentage of market capitalisation of 69.8 percent compared to 53.4 in Britain, 40.3 in Malaysia and 31.3 percent in Hong Kong.
He put the percentage at 99.9 for Germany followed by New York Stock Exchange's 89.2 percent.
